chapters.title: Chapter 2: Theories of Exchange Rate Determination

lessons.title: Purchasing Power Parity: Why the Rupee "Should" Weaken Over Time

children.text: A McDonald's Big Mac costs roughly ₹230 in an Indian metro and around $5.50 in a major US city. Convert ₹230 into dollars at a typical USD/INR rate and you get about $2.75, half the US price for what is meant to be an identical burger. Either Indian McDonald's franchisees are running a permanent charity operation, or the rupee is trading at a level that does not reflect what it can actually buy. Economists have a name for the theory that says this gap should not persist forever: purchasing power parity.

body.text: Purchasing power parity (PPP) says exchange rates should adjust over time so that the same basket of goods costs the same amount everywhere, once converted into a common currency. Where a country's prices rise faster than another's, PPP predicts that country's currency should weaken to compensate.

children.text: The Law of One Price: The Building Block of PPP

markDefs.definition: The idea that in a frictionless market, with no transport costs or trade barriers, an identical good should sell for the same price everywhere once converted into a common currency. PPP is this law applied to an entire basket of goods across a whole economy.

children.text: PPP rests on a simpler idea called the

: if the same good can be freely traded, with no shipping costs or import duties, it should sell for the same price everywhere once converted into a common currency. If gold trades cheaper in Mumbai than in London after converting at the market exchange rate, traders would buy gold in Mumbai and sell it in London until the gap closes. PPP takes this logic and applies it to an entire economy's basket of goods and services rather than one traded commodity, which is exactly where it starts to run into trouble, as you will see later in this lesson.

is the strict version: the exchange rate should exactly equal the ratio of price levels between two countries, so that an identical basket of goods costs the same in rupees or dollars once converted. This almost never holds precisely in practice, price levels are hard to compare basket-for-basket across two very different economies, so it is treated more as a benchmark than a forecast.

is the version actually used in practice, and it is far more useful. Instead of comparing absolute price levels, it looks at the difference in inflation rates between two countries and predicts how the exchange rate should move over time. If India's inflation consistently runs higher than US inflation, relative PPP says the rupee should depreciate against the dollar by roughly that same gap each year, simply to keep the relative cost of goods in balance.

body.caption: Relative PPP: the rupee's expected percentage depreciation against the dollar approximately equals India's inflation rate minus the US inflation rate.

cells: Price levels of an identical basket across two countries, in a common currency
A conceptual benchmark for "fair value"; rarely holds exactly
The gap between two countries' inflation rates, over time
A practical rule of thumb for the direction and rough pace of long-run currency drift

children.text: The Big Mac Index: PPP Made Visible

markDefs.definition: An informal index published by The Economist magazine since 1986, comparing the price of a McDonald's Big Mac across countries, converted to a common currency, as a light-hearted but genuinely useful gauge of PPP.

children.text: takes this exact logic and applies it to one standardised product sold in almost identical form worldwide. A Big Mac in India has historically priced out cheaper in dollar terms than a Big Mac in the US, implying, by this rough measure, that the rupee trades below its PPP-implied fair value. This does not mean the rupee is "wrong" or about to snap back to that fair value; it mostly reflects that India's overall cost structure, especially cheaper labour and rent, sits well below the US even after adjusting for the exchange rate. That gap between a country's actual price level and PPP's predicted level is completely normal and can persist for decades.

children.text: Why PPP Fails to Hold in the Short Run

markDefs.definition: Goods and services that cannot easily be shipped across borders and arbitraged, like a haircut, a restaurant meal, or urban rent. These make up a large share of any economy's price basket and never face the international price pressure PPP assumes.

children.text: PPP assumes goods can be freely arbitraged across borders, but a large share of what any household actually spends money on, rent, haircuts, restaurant meals, domestic transport, falls under

. No one is shipping haircuts from Mumbai to New York to arbitrage away a price gap, so these prices never get pulled into line the way tradable goods do. Add in tariffs, transport costs and different consumption baskets across countries, and absolute PPP never really has a chance to hold exactly. On top of that, in the short run, currency markets are dominated by capital flows, interest rate decisions and risk sentiment, forces that move billions of dollars in minutes, completely overwhelming the slow, structural pull of inflation differentials that PPP describes.

body.title: PPP: Short Run vs. Long Run

columns.label: Short Run (weeks to months)
points: Dominated by capital flows, interest rate moves and risk sentiment
PPP deviations can widen or persist for years without correcting
Not useful as a trading signal on its own
A currency can look "cheap" or "expensive" by PPP and stay that way indefinitely

columns.label: Long Run (years to decades)
points: Inflation differentials gradually pull real exchange rates back toward parity
Useful as a rough anchor for "fair value" over a multi-year horizon
Explains why persistently high-inflation currencies tend to depreciate structurally
Forms the theoretical basis for real effective exchange rate (REER) analysis

body.title: PPP-Implied USD/INR Path at a 3% Inflation Differential

body.text: Do not use PPP to time a currency trade. It says almost nothing about where USD/INR will be next week or next quarter, capital flows and interest rate expectations dominate that horizon completely. PPP is a long-run anchor for thinking about structural currency drift, not a short-term signal.

body.title: Apply Relative PPP
body.prompt: India's inflation is running at 6% and US inflation is at 2%. Today's spot USD/INR is ₹83.00. Using relative PPP (the approximate rule: expected depreciation equals the inflation differential), what should USD/INR be roughly one year from now?
body.explanation: The inflation differential is 6% minus 2% = 4%. Applying this to today's spot rate: ₹83.00 x 1.04 = ₹86.32. (The more precise compounding version, 83 x 1.06/1.02, gives ₹86.25, close enough that the simple approximation is what practitioners actually use day to day.)

body.title: Did the 2013 Taper Tantrum Break PPP?
body.scenario: In mid-2013, when the US Federal Reserve signalled it would start reducing its bond-buying programme, the rupee fell sharply against the dollar within a matter of weeks, a much larger and faster move than any change in India-US inflation differentials over that period could explain.
body.prompt: Does this episode disprove purchasing power parity? What does it actually tell you about the time horizon over which PPP is meant to operate, and what was really driving the rupee's move instead?
body.modelAnswer: It does not disprove PPP, it illustrates PPP's limits. PPP describes a slow, structural relationship that plays out over years, tied to the accumulated gap between two countries' inflation rates. The 2013 move was driven by a sudden shift in capital flows: foreign investors pulled money out of Indian debt and equity markets in anticipation of higher US interest rates, a capital account shock that has nothing to do with the price of a haircut in Mumbai versus New York. Short-run currency moves are overwhelmingly driven by capital flows and interest rate expectations, not inflation differentials. PPP is the right tool for asking "where should the rupee trend over the next five to ten years," and the wrong tool for explaining a six-week move.

points: Purchasing power parity says exchange rates should adjust so that an identical basket of goods costs the same everywhere, once converted to a common currency. It rests on the law of one price applied to an entire economy.

Absolute PPP compares price levels directly and rarely holds exactly. Relative PPP, comparing inflation differentials over time, is the practically useful version: higher domestic inflation implies a currency should depreciate roughly in line with that gap.
The Big Mac Index is a simplified, real-world illustration of PPP using one standardised product, and persistent gaps from PPP-implied fair value are normal, not a sign the theory is broken.
PPP breaks down in the short run because of non-tradable goods, trade barriers, and because capital flows and interest rate expectations dominate currency moves over weeks and months.
Treat PPP as a long-run anchor for structural currency drift over years, never as a short-term trading signal.
